base.notes: The South Dakota class (1920) was completed as drawn — the last design of the 1916 program, and the only capital ships aboard which nothing of the escalation grammar was ever fitted. The eight modernized Standards carry the standard-type modernization of 1926-33, sheeted in docs/hindsight/inherited-hulls-catalog.md: Colorado x3, Tennessee x2, New Mexico x3. Six Standards sit in reserve with crews stripped for the United States class in 1933-35: Pennsylvania x2, Nevada x2, New York x2. The four older dreadnoughts in training and mothballs are DERIVED, not stated in canon: Florida, Utah, Wyoming and Arkansas, on the reading that Delaware and North Dakota went under the treaty's scrap-on-replacement clause when the Missouris commissioned. Langley is the training deck. Nothing in the base file is edited.

not_built.why: Under 4 percent of the appropriation. One purpose-built carrier, one air group, ~260 carrier-qualified pilots, and a pipeline adding ~40 a year through Ranger's single deck.
One sonar set issued as budgets allowed, one depth charge, no thrower and no ahead-thrown weapon in service.

THE FLEET DOES NOT PROVISION. No American hull carries a mast, a wiring run or a power margin drawn for a set that does not yet exist, so every later fit is structural work at structural prices. This is the exact inverse of the Japanese divergence and is the point of the contrast.

not_built.what: A fourth set of locks, or the Nicaragua canal
not_built.why: Both studies complete, both unfunded, in the same desk drawer as the carrier memo.

not_built.what: Any reactive program against a rival

classes.name: Constitution class
classes.changes: +14,000 t standard; +33 m length, beam unchanged, +0.5 m draft; Mark 1 turrets, 18 in for 16 in — the ladder's first caliber step, same four groups, same 100 rpg, firing time 80 → 67 min on a faster gun; secondary unchanged; +4 high-angle guns and machine guns added, the first close-in battery on the ladder; +18,000 shp on the same twelve boilers, still turbo-electric, still four shafts, speed unchanged at 25 kt; belt +26 mm, deck +26 mm, barbettes +51 mm, turret faces +51 mm; torpedo defense 0.5 m deeper; +1,000 t oil; crew +600; cost +8,000 gold, durability +1,700. ⚠ And the one that is not on the sheet: at 8.89 lengths to the beam she is the finest capital hull ever drawn, because the canal will not let her be wider. classes.name: Ranger

provisions.notes: Two flush-deck catapult track foundations — the one provision in the whole fleet, and it is for a catapult.

classes.notes: The fleet's carrier doctrine entire: one deck, one air group, and the whole of the service's flight-deck practice. The deck park handles and ranges rather than stows, and it is generous BECAUSE NOTHING ABOARD FOLDS. She was built once, and the drawings were put away. Fire control as launched is optical sights.

classes.name: Astoria class

spec.name: 8 in/55 pattern 1926
spec.notes: Outside the Mark sequence: the escalation ladder retooled one gun plant upward and the cruiser battery was never part of it.

features: belt over the machinery box only

classes.notes: The scouting line: the eyes the battle line's gunnery doctrine requires, and the escort the spotting aircraft work behind. Fire control as launched is 2 x 8 in director tops with 5 m rangefinders. Her protection assumes she will not have to take an action for long.

classes.name: Farragut class

None of the listening gear the doctrine assumes, because the listening gear was not in the appropriation.

classes.notes: The first ship in the fleet whose battery fights aircraft and surface targets with the same barrels under one director. She screens the battle line, and the doctrine has never asked what happens when she is not there.

classes.name: Dolphin class

provisions.notes: Passive hydrophones of 1926 pattern; no echo-ranging set.

classes.notes: The requirement was written from the war plan backwards: the patrol radius came first and the rest of the boat was sized to it. Drawn to run surfaced and dive to attack, so the diesel plant and the bunkerage are the design's dominant weights and the battery is sized for an approach rather than for an evasion. Motors 3,600 shp. Fire control is a mechanical torpedo angle solver in the conning tower. Fuel figure includes fuel-ballast tanks.

aircraft.name: F1 carrier fighter
features: biplane on an all-metal airframe with fabric-covered flying surfaces
2 x cowl 7.62 mm machine guns, 1,000 rounds
2 x 45 kg bombs on wing racks
aircraft.notes: The carrier arm's air-defense doctrine entire: intercept on sight from a deck alert, with no radar, no direction organization and no vector but the eye. Its guns are of rifle caliber. Endurance rather than speed or climb is what the specification bought, because the fleet states its aviation problem as a scouting problem. It is what a carrier strike would be met with. No successor specification has been issued.

aircraft.name: SB1 scout-bomber

crew.notes: Tandem. The second crewman is the point of the design: he navigates the search leg, works the radio and fights the tail.

aircraft.notes: The carrier arm's strike and its scouting line at once, and the whole of the service's practical experience of delivering a weapon from a deck. The doctrine it wrote is the only aviation doctrine the gunnery fleet has consented to fund. No successor specification.

aircraft.name: O1 observation floatplane

crew.notes: Tandem. The radio-plot station in the rear cockpit was the requirement's first line, and the airframe followed it.

features: wings fold for the catapult ships' handling arrangements
1 x cowl 7.62 mm + 1 x flexible rear 7.62 mm machine gun, 1,100 rounds
2 x 50 kg bombs on wing racks
aircraft.notes: The eyes of the gunnery doctrine: launched over the horizon, holding station above the fall of shot, passing corrections to the plot by radio — which is what makes fire at extreme range a solved problem rather than a hope. Printed figures are the float fit; the wheel fit gives the penalty back. In a service where the floatplane path is the elite path, this is the airframe that path is flown in. Deliveries begin spring 1936. FOURTH WEIGHT,: the printed max is the FLOAT state, because she is a floatplane; [us36flt] exchanges to wheels, and that kit's own row carries the saving.

construction.notes: Appropriation ~120,000 gold a year; the ladder and its plant take ~65%, naval aviation under 4%. FIVE generations of THREE hulls each, laid 1923-1935: a new and larger generation every two years, the interval constant and the class size constant, with the BORE the only variable and each bore mounted in two generations.

fuel.notes: Fuel, steel and money are no constraint — this is the richest navy on Earth. What is scarce is permission.

pools.notes: The pipeline runs through Ranger's one deck.
Where careers are made. The floatplane corps is the world's best.

schools: gunnery (the world's finest, and they know it)
manpower.notes: THE CASCADE, AND IT IS NOW THE SCENARIO RATHER THAN A PRESSURE INSIDE IT. Ten commissioned monsters hold 36,050 men, better than a quarter of the whole Navy. Commissioning the three United States hulls in 1933-35 took ~12,450 berths, found by emptying the six reserve Standards and sending four older dreadnoughts to training and mothballs; that pool is spent. The five hulls still building need about 34,000 berths - which is, to a rounding error, the entire complement of the pre-escalation battle line. Finishing the ships already begun means paying off every capital ship the Navy owned before the ladder started.

infrastructure.notes: Passes the Missouris at 33.2 m beam and 12.3 m draft, with fenders breathing in, and no capital ship built since.

Opened 1934. Usable 360 x 44.0 m, over-sill 13.7 m. Passes the United States class fully (38.5 m beam, 12.4 m draft) and nothing else ever built; FAILS THE TILLMANS at 44.5 m beam by half a meter, and the Columbias at 46.5 m by two and a half. A beam does not defuel: there is no light-transit case.
Fifth-generation. Complete 1937. One of only two docks on Earth that will hold a Columbia.
16 in and 18 in lines warm; 21.5 in proven and in production — the plant was retooled twice in nine years and stands retooled for a bore nobody has ordered.
Capacity quadrupled 1922-30; three mills, order books full to 1939. THE BINDING CONSTRAINT ON THE WHOLE LADDER, and the one number nobody outside the country has.
Plus monster ways at four private and two navy yards.

objectives: Keep the ladder's drawer from ever being empty

notes: The escalation ladder is FIVE generations of THREE hulls each - Missouri 1923, Constitution 1925, United States 1927, Tillman 1929, Columbia 1932 - on THREE CALIBERS and TWO MARKS: the 16 in 1918 pattern (outside the Mark sequence, a literal spec), the 18 in Mark 1 [us25gun] and the 21.5 in Mark 2 [us29gun], TRIPLES throughout. Twenty-five knots on every rung and it never moves. The cadence law lives at the scenario file's section 2.1.
